# Pilot — GOV.UK services

**Real data.** Generated by `tools/adapters/services-govuk.py` from the GOV.UK search and
content APIs.

```bash
python3 tools/adapters/services-govuk.py --limit 40 --out examples/pilot-govuk-services
```

40 services from 15 departments, drawn from the 240 transactions GOV.UK publishes.

**GOV.UK does not use HSDS**, which is the point. An Open Referral publisher would mostly
verify the crosswalk table; this asks whether the profile can represent a real catalogue built
on entirely different assumptions.

## The headline finding: 12 of 18 fields, and the gap is structural

| Filled 40/40 | Filled 0/40 |
|---|---|
| `name`, `description`, `url`, `provider`, `areaServed` | `eligibility` |
| `serviceStatus`, `lifeEvent`, `keywords` | `requiredDocument` |
| `applicationProcess`, `availableChannel` | `cost` |
| `availableLanguage`, `dateModified` | `processingTime` |
| | `availableAtLocation`, `relatedLegislation` |

The six empty fields are not missing information. **They are information GOV.UK publishes as
prose rather than as data:**

```
processingTime present in prose but not as a field   12 of 40
eligibility     present in prose but not as a field    8 of 40
cost            present in prose but not as a field    3 of 40
other ways to apply published as prose, not channels   8 of 40
```

A page reads *"Use this service to tax your car, motorcycle or other vehicle using a reference
number from: a recent vehicle tax reminder … your vehicle log book (V5C) — it must be in your
name"*. That is eligibility and required documents, written for a human being. There is no
field carrying either.

**The profile assumed publishers hold this structured. The best-organised government service
catalogue in the world does not.** That is worth stating plainly rather than treating as a
conversion shortfall.

The adapter does **not** parse the prose into structure. Extracting a fee from a sentence
produces a number nobody checked, and the profile would rather have a gap than a figure it
cannot vouch for — the same position the elections pilot took on turnout.

## What the profile got right

`applicationProcess` is free text by design, which is why it fills 40 of 40 while the
structured fields sit empty. Had it been modelled as a structured sequence, GOV.UK's narrative
would have been unrepresentable and the most useful thing on the page would have been lost.

`lifeEvent` inferred cleanly for 35 of 40 from GOV.UK's topic taxonomy — adjacent, not
identical, and the mapping is reported rather than silent. Five services yielded nothing and
fall back to `other`.

## The defect

**Every service was attributed to the Government Digital Service.**

The content API exposes both `primary_publishing_organisation` and `organisations`. The first
is who publishes the *page* — on GOV.UK mainstream content that is always GDS. The second is
the department that owns the *service*: DVLA, DWP, Companies House, the Home Office.

The adapter preferred the first, producing one provider for forty services and making the
field useless. Corrected, the same forty services resolve to **15 real departments**.

The distinction matters beyond this pilot: any catalogue that separates publishing from
ownership can be read either way, and only one of the readings is useful.

## Not applicable here

`availableAtLocation` is empty because GOV.UK services are digital and national — there is no
counter to attend. That is the profile behaving correctly rather than a gap; the field exists
for services delivered in person, which the HSDS-derived model is largely about.
